The problem asks whether there exists N with one 1990-term representation and exactly 1990 total positive-consecutive representations.

milestones.description: Let N=a+(a+1)+\cdots+(a+k-1) with integers a\ge1 and k\ge2. Prove that 2N=k(2a+k-1). Deduce that if k is odd then k divides N, and if k is even then k divides 2N but does not divide N, so the odd number 2a+k-1 equals 2N/k.
milestones.answer: 2N=k(2a+k-1). Hence for odd k, k\mid N. For even k, writing k=2m gives N=m(2a+k-1), where 2a+k-1 is odd; equivalently 2N/k=2a+k-1 is an odd integer.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the algebraic identity is shown and the odd/even divisibility conclusions are correctly stated. Minor equivalent formulations are fine.
hints: Use the average of the first and last terms: N=k\cdot(2a+k-1)/2.
When k is odd, gcd(k,2)=1, so k\mid 2N implies k\mid N.

milestones.description: Prove the converse classification: for a positive integer N, every representation N=a+(a+1)+\cdots+(a+k-1) with a\ge1 and k\ge2 corresponds to an odd divisor d of N via one of the two cases below, and every odd divisor d>1 of N gives at most one such representation. The two cases are: (1) odd length k=d, which is valid exactly when a=N/d-(d-1)/2 is at least 1; (2) even length k=2N/d, where d is an odd divisor of N, which is valid exactly when a=(d-k+1)/2 is at least 1. Conclude that the total number of representations of N as a sum of one or more consecutive positive integers equals the number of odd divisors of N.
milestones.answer: There is a bijection between representations of N as sums of one or more consecutive positive integers and odd divisors of N: each odd divisor d of N yields exactly one valid representation, either of odd length d or of even length 2N/d. Therefore the number of such representations equals the number of odd divisors of N.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver states the standard odd-divisor classification with explicit formulas for a and the conclusion that the count of representations into one or more consecutive positive integers equals the number of odd divisors. The positivity condition may be handled by choosing the valid one of the two lengths for each odd divisor.
decompose_advice: First show how a given representation produces an odd divisor d of N using the identity 2N=k(2a+k-1).
Then, for a fixed odd divisor d of N, compare d with \sqrt{2N} to decide whether the valid length is d or 2N/d, and verify a\ge1.

milestones.description: Using the fact that the number of representations of N as a sum of one or more consecutive positive integers equals the number of odd divisors of N, and noting that the one-term representation N=N must be excluded because the problem asks for more than one term, express f(N) in terms of the number of odd divisors of N. Then translate the condition f(N)=1990 into an exact statement about the number of odd divisors of N.

milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the response correctly subtracts the one-term representation and concludes that N must have exactly 1991 odd divisors.

So 'exactly 1990 ways with more than one term' means '1991 ways with one or more terms'.

milestones.description: Assume N can be written as a sum of 1990 consecutive integers: N=b+(b+1)+\cdots+(b+1989) for some integer b. Compute N in terms of b, and prove from this formula that 1990 divides N. Then deduce that the odd part of N is divisible by 995.
milestones.answer: N=1990b+\frac{1990\cdot1989}{2}=1990(b+994.5)=995(2b+1989), so 1990\mid N. Since 1990=2\cdot995 and 995 is odd, the odd part of N is divisible by 995.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver derives N=1990(b+994.5) or an equivalent formula, concludes 1990\mid N, and states that the odd part of N is a multiple of 995. Equivalent algebraic forms are fine.

Because the number of terms 1990 is even, the average is a half-integer, but the total is still an integer multiple of 1990.

milestones.description: Let the odd part of N be M, so N=2^t M with M odd. From the previous condition, 995 divides M. Write the prime factorization 995=5\cdot199. Prove that any odd positive integer divisible by 995 has at least (1+1)(1+1)=4 positive divisors coming just from the exponents of 5 and 199, and conclude that M cannot have exactly 1991 positive divisors if 1991 is prime.
milestones.answer: Since 995=5\cdot199 divides M, the divisor count of M is at least 4. If M had exactly 1991 divisors and 1991 is prime, then M would have to be a prime power, whose divisor count has the form e+1=1991; but a prime power cannot be divisible by two distinct primes 5 and 199. So M cannot have exactly 1991 divisors.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the argument uses that divisor counts multiply over prime exponents and that a number with prime divisor count 1991 must be a prime power. The conclusion should be that no such odd part M exists.
hints: If M=\prod p_i^{e_i}, then the number of positive divisors is \prod (e_i+1).
Because 1991 is prime, the only way to get divisor count 1991 is a single factor e+1=1991.

milestones.answer: 1991 is prime.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver correctly verifies no listed prime divides 1991. A concise check is fine; for example, 1991 is odd, digit sum 20 so not divisible by 3, does not end in 5, and direct remainders exclude the remaining primes.

Explain why the argument only used the 1990-term condition to deduce 1990\mid N and did not need b to be positive.

The counting formula for f(N) applies only to positive-term sums and was introduced separately.

But the odd part M is divisible by 5 and by 199, so it cannot be a power of one prime.

milestones.description: Let the two integer roots of the quadratic equation x^2-pqx+p+q=0 be r and s, where p and q are natural numbers. Using Vieta’s formulas for a monic quadratic x^2-(sum)x+(product)=0, write the system of equations relating r,s,p,q, and restate the goal entirely in terms of finding natural numbers p,q for which there exist integers r,s satisfying that system.

milestones.description: Suppose integers r and s satisfy rs=p+q with p and q natural numbers. Prove that r and s must have the same sign, and in fact both are positive integers. Also use r+s=pq with p,q natural to rule out the possibility that both are negative.

milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer concludes r,s are positive integers via rs>0 and r+s>0.

Two integers with positive product have the same sign.

milestones.description: Let r and s be positive integers satisfying r+s=pq and rs=p+q. Starting from rs=p+q and r+s=pq, derive an identity that factors as (pr-1)(ps-1)=p^2-1. The derivation must be explicit and self-contained.
milestones.answer: Using q=rs-p from rs=p+q, substitute into r+s=pq to get r+s=p(rs-p)=prs-p^2, so prs-r-s=p^2. Adding 1 gives prs-r-s+1=p^2+1-? More directly, (pr-1)(ps-1)=p^2rs-p(r+s)+1=p^2(p+q)-p(pq)+1=p^3+p^2q-p^2q+1=p^3+1 is wrong, so instead use rs=p+q and r+s=pq: (pr-1)(ps-1)=p^2rs-p(r+s)+1=p^2(p+q)-p(pq)+1=p^3+p^2q-p^2q+1=p^3+1. Hence this route is not correct; the correct factorization is (p-r)(p-s)=p^2-pq+p+q.
milestones.note: ACCEPT ONLY IF the milestone identifies that the attempted factorization (pr-1)(ps-1)=p^2-1 is false and replaces it with the correct identity (p-r)(p-s)=p^2-pq+p+q, or an equivalent correct transformed identity derived from Vieta. Reject the incorrect claimed formula.

Then choose a factorization that can be used to bound or solve for p and q.

milestones.description: Assume positive integers r,s,p,q satisfy r+s=pq and rs=p+q. Derive the correct identity (r-p)(s-p)=q(p-1)-p^2. Then, by symmetry, also derive (r-q)(s-q)=p(q-1)-q^2. These are algebraic restatements only.
milestones.answer: (r-p)(s-p)=rs-p(r+s)+p^2=(p+q)-p(pq)+p^2=q(p-1)-p^2. Similarly, (r-q)(s-q)=rs-q(r+s)+q^2=(p+q)-q(pq)+q^2=p(q-1)-q^2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF both displayed identities are derived correctly from rs=p+q and r+s=pq.

If one identity is enough, the symmetric one can be kept as a backup.

milestones.description: Let r and s be positive integers with r+s=pq. Prove that at least one of r and s is at most pq/2. Then use rs=p+q to show that if p>=3 and q>=3, a contradiction follows. All needed equations are: r+s=pq and rs=p+q.
milestones.answer: Since r+s=pq, at least one root is at most pq/2; say r<=pq/2. Then s=pq-r>=pq/2, so rs=r(pq-r) is at most (pq/2)^2 by the product bound for fixed sum, but more simply rs>=r and does not immediately contradict. Using the standard bound for fixed sum, rs<=((pq)^2)/4. Thus p+q=rs<=p^2q^2/4, which alone is not a contradiction. So this route is insufficient; one needs a sharper argument.

Check whether p+q<=p^2q^2/4 can ever contradict p,q>=3.

milestones.description: Because the original equation and the conditions are symmetric in p and q, explain why one may assume without loss of generality that p<=q. Then split into the cases p=1, p=2, and p>=3, with the understanding that all solutions with p>q can be recovered by symmetry.

Then show no solutions exist when p>=3 under p<=q.

milestones.description: Assume p=1. The equation becomes x^2-qx+q+1=0. If its roots are integers r and s, then r+s=q and rs=q+1. Solve completely for all natural numbers q for which this is possible.
milestones.answer: From r+s=q and rs=q+1, substitute q=r+s into rs=q+1 to get rs=r+s+1, so (r-1)(s-1)=2. Since r,s are positive integers, the possibilities are (r-1,s-1)=(1,2) or (2,1), giving (r,s)=(2,3) or (3,2). Hence q=r+s=5. So the only solution with p=1 is q=5.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF q=5 is obtained uniquely for p=1, with equivalent factorization or direct checking.
hints: Use q=r+s in rs=q+1.
Factor rs-r-s=1 as (r-1)(s-1)=2.

milestones.description: Assume p=2. The equation becomes x^2-2qx+q+2=0. If its roots are integers r and s, then r+s=2q and rs=q+2. Solve completely for all natural numbers q for which this is possible.
milestones.answer: From r+s=2q and rs=q+2, substitute q=(r+s)/2 into rs=q+2 to get 2rs=r+s+4. Rearranging, 4rs-2r-2s=8, so (2r-1)(2s-1)=9. Since r,s are positive integers, the positive odd factor pairs of 9 are (1,9),(3,3),(9,1), giving (r,s)=(1,5),(2,2),(5,1). These correspond to q=(r+s)/2 equal to 3, 2, and 3. Hence the solutions with p=2 are q=2 and q=3.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF q=2 and q=3 are found exactly for p=2.
hints: Eliminate q using q=(r+s)/2.
Complete a factorization in the odd variables 2r-1 and 2s-1.

milestones.description: Assume p<=q and p>=3. Let the integer roots be r,s, so r+s=pq and rs=p+q. Prove that no such solution exists by using the inequality rs>=r+s-1 for positive integers r,s, with equality only if one root is 1. Combine this with rs=p+q and r+s=pq.
milestones.answer: For positive integers r,s, write rs-(r+s-1)=(r-1)(s-1)>=0, so rs>=r+s-1. Here this gives p+q=rs>=pq-1, hence pq-p-q<=1, so (p-1)(q-1)<=2. Under p<=q and p>=3, we have (p-1)(q-1)>=2(q-1)>=4, contradiction. Therefore no solutions exist for p>=3.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the argument derives p+q>=pq-1, equivalently (p-1)(q-1)<=2, and then contradicts p>=3<=q.
hints: Use (r-1)(s-1)>=0 for positive integers r,s.
Rewrite pq-p-q<=1 as (p-1)(q-1)<=2.

milestones.description: Assemble the established casework. The relevant facts are: by symmetry one may assume p<=q; if p=1, the only possibility is q=5; if p=2, the possibilities are q=2 and q=3; if p>=3, there are no solutions. State all natural-number pairs (p,q) for which the roots of x^2-pqx+p+q=0 are integers, including symmetric pairs with p>q.

milestones.description: Let d=mn-1. Rewrite the divisibility condition in the problem as a congruence modulo d, and state the goal in this language. The original problem is to determine all strictly positive integer pairs (m,n) such that mn-1 divides n^3-1.

Since m,n are positive integers, d=mn-1 is a positive integer except when m=n=1 gives d=0, which must be handled separately.

The expression 0 | 0 is not allowed in standard integer divisibility.

milestones.description: Assume from now on that mn-1>0 and let d=mn-1. Using the congruence mn≡1 (mod d), prove that m^3(n^3-1)≡1-m^3 (mod d). Then use the fact that d divides n^3-1 to deduce that d divides m^3-1.
milestones.answer: Since mn≡1 (mod d), cubing gives m^3n^3≡1 (mod d). Hence m^3(n^3-1)=m^3n^3-m^3≡1-m^3 (mod d). If d|n^3-1, then d|m^3(n^3-1), so d|(1-m^3), equivalently d|m^3-1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver derives d|m^3-1 from d=mn-1 and d|n^3-1 via the displayed congruence.

Then separately combine d|n^3-1 with the congruence for m^3(n^3-1).

milestones.description: Let d=mn-1 with mn-1>0. Suppose d divides both n^3-1 and m^3-1. Prove that d divides (mn)^3-1, and then prove that d divides m^3+n^3. You may use the identity (mn)^3-1=m^3n^3-1=m^3(n^3-1)+(m^3-1).
milestones.answer: Because d divides n^3-1 and m^3-1, the identity (mn)^3-1=m^3(n^3-1)+(m^3-1) shows d|(mn)^3-1. Since mn=d+1, we have (mn)^3-1=(d+1)^3-1=d(d^2+3d+3), so d|(mn)^3-1. Also (mn)^3-1=(mn-1)(m^2n^2+mn+1)=d(m^2n^2+mn+1). Comparing with m^3n^3-1=(m^3-1)(n^3-1)+(m^3-1)+(n^3-1), one gets d|(m^3-1)+(n^3-1)=m^3+n^3-2; together with d|(mn)^3-1=(d+1)^3-1 gives the cleaner congruence mn≡1 mod d, so m^3n^3≡1 mod d and from n^3≡1 mod d we get m^3≡1 mod d. Therefore m^3+n^3≡2 mod d, i.e. d|m^3+n^3-2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver correctly proves d|(mn)^3-1 and concludes the useful congruence m^3+n^3≡2 mod d (equivalently d|m^3+n^3-2).

Then convert the divisibility information into congruences modulo d and add them.

milestones.description:
Assume mn-1>0 and d=mn-1 divides both m^3-1 and n^3-1. Use the factorization x^3-1=(x-1)(x^2+x+1) to prove that d divides both (m-1)(m^2+m+1) and (n-1)(n^2+n+1). Then show that d divides the integer
(m-1)(n^2+n+1)+m(n-1)(m^2+m+1), and simplify this integer completely in terms of m+n and d.
milestones.answer:
d divides (m-1)(m^2+m+1) and (n-1)(n^2+n+1), hence it divides
(m-1)(n^2+n+1)+m(n-1)(m^2+m+1).
A direct expansion simplifies this to (m+n)(mn-1)=(m+n)d. So d divides (m+n)d, which is automatic.

Then expand the proposed linear combination carefully and collect terms to factor out mn-1.

milestones.description: Assume mn-1>0 and d=mn-1 divides n^3-1. Since d=mn-1 is positive, prove the inequality d≤n^3-1. Deduce that m≤(n^3)/(n)=n^2+1/n, and hence, because m is an integer, m≤n^2. By symmetry from the result that d also divides m^3-1, deduce n≤m^2.

milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver derives m≤n^2 and n≤m^2 from positivity and divisibility. Minor inequality variations are fine.

Use d=mn-1<n^3 to get mn≤n^3 because mn is an integer.

milestones.description:
Assume m≤n. With d=mn-1 and d|n^3-1, divide n^3-1 by mn-1 as a polynomial in n with parameter m:

n^3-1=(mn-1)Q+R,

where Q and R are explicit integer expressions in m and n and the remainder R is linear in n. Compute such a decomposition and use it to prove that mn-1 divides m^2+n+m.
milestones.answer:
We have
n^3-1=(mn-1)·n/m? not integral, so instead use the exact identity
m^2(n^3-1)=(mn-1)(mn^2+n+m)+m+n-(m^3+1).
Using the earlier fact mn-1|m^3-1 and mn-1|n^3-1, this yields mn-1|m+n-2. Equivalently, a cleaner standard decomposition is
n^3-1=(mn-1)(⌊n^2/m⌋\text{ not useful})+\text{remainder},
so the intended usable conclusion is mn-1|m^3-1 and mn-1|n^3-1, hence mn-1 divides any integer combination of them; in particular,
(n^3-1)-n(mn-1)(n-m)=n^2m^2+\cdots,
leading to mn-1|m^2+n+m.
milestones.note: ACCEPT ONLY IF the solver produces a correct explicit decomposition proving mn-1 | (m^2+n+m) or an equivalent small positive expression. Reject vague polynomial division without a valid identity.

If your decomposition is not exact, split further until every algebraic identity is verified term-by-term.

milestones.description: Assume m≤n and also that mn-1 divides the positive integer m+n-2. Use the inequality mn-1≤m+n-2 to show that (m-1)(n-1)≤0. Since m,n are positive integers and m≤n, deduce all possibilities for m and then solve for n from the original divisibility condition.
milestones.answer: From mn-1≤m+n-2 we get mn-m-n+1≤0, i.e. (m-1)(n-1)≤0. With positive integers and m≤n, this forces m=1. Then the condition becomes n-1|n^3-1. Since n^3-1=(n-1)(n^2+n+1), every positive integer n works. Under m≤n this gives all pairs (1,n) with n≥1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the solver derives m=1 under m≤n and then checks that every n gives a solution. Must still respect the earlier exclusion of (1,1) only if divisibility by 0 arose there; here m=1 gives divisor n-1, so n=1 is excluded because the divisor is 0.
hints: Rewrite mn-1≤m+n-2 as mn-m-n+1≤0.
Factor mn-m-n+1=(m-1)(n-1).

milestones.description: Assemble the previous facts into the full solution set. You may use these established statements: (i) (1,1) is excluded because mn-1=0; (ii) for any solution with mn-1>0, the same divisor mn-1 divides both n^3-1 and m^3-1; (iii) after ordering the pair so that m≤n, one obtains mn-1 divides m+n-2; (iv) this forces m=1; (v) with m=1, the condition becomes n-1|n^3-1, which holds for every integer n>1. Convert this back to all ordered pairs (m,n) of positive integers.
milestones.answer: The solutions are exactly all pairs (m,n)=(1,n) with n≥2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final set is exactly {(1,n): n≥2}. Reject any answer including (1,1) or pairs with m>1.
hints: Use the ordering step only as a temporary WLOG device, then translate back to ordered pairs.
Check directly that if m=1 and n≥2, then n-1 divides n^3-1 because n^3-1=(n-1)(n^2+n+1).

milestones.description: Let g(z)=a z+b, where f(z)=a z^2+b z+c is a complex polynomial satisfying |f(z)|≤1 for every complex number z with |z|≤1. Express g(z) in terms of f'(z), and restate the goal as finding the largest possible value of |g(z)| on the unit disk under the hypothesis |f(z)|≤1 on the unit disk.
milestones.answer: Since f'(z)=2a z+b, we have g(z)=a z+b=(f'(z)+b)/2, but the more useful relation is g(z)=f'(z)-a z. The goal is to determine the sharp bound for |a z+b| when |z|≤1, given |f(z)|≤1 on |z|≤1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the response identifies the object to bound as g(z)=a z+b and restates the task as finding its maximal possible modulus on the unit disk under the given boundedness of f. Exact choice of derivative relation need not be unique.
decompose_advice: Introduce a standard coefficient estimate for bounded analytic functions on the unit disk.
Then derive separate bounds on a and b from that estimate.

milestones.description: Suppose h(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n z^n is analytic on |z|<1 and satisfies |h(z)|≤1 for all |z|<1. Using Cauchy's integral formula for coefficients, show that every coefficient satisfies |c_n|≤1. This is a standalone fact you may use later.
milestones.answer: For every n≥0, |c_n|≤1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF they state the standard Cauchy estimate for coefficients of a function bounded by 1 on the unit disk. A brief derivation via c_n=(1/2πi)∮ h(ζ)/ζ^{n+1} dζ is enough.
hints: Then |c_n|≤r^{-n}; let r→1^- to get |c_n|≤1.

milestones.description: Apply the coefficient bound from the previous standalone fact to the quadratic polynomial f(z)=a z^2+b z+c satisfying |f(z)|≤1 for |z|≤1. Determine explicit bounds for |a| and |b|.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF both coefficient bounds are obtained correctly from the boundedness of f on the unit disk.
hints: In the power series of f, the coefficient of z^2 is a and the coefficient of z is b.
Use the fact that every coefficient of a bounded analytic function on the unit disk has modulus at most 1.

milestones.description: Let u and v be complex numbers with |u|≤1 and |v|≤1. For any complex number z with |z|≤1, prove that |u z+v|≤|u||z|+|v|≤2. This gives a universal bound for a z+b once separate bounds on |a| and |b| are known.
milestones.answer: If |u|≤1, |v|≤1, and |z|≤1, then |u z+v|≤2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the triangle inequality is used to derive |u z+v|≤|u||z|+|v|≤2.
hints: Use |u z+v|≤|u z|+|v|.
Then use |u z|=|u||z|≤|u|≤1.

milestones.description: Using only the facts |a|≤1 and |b|≤1 and the inequality |u z+v|≤2 for |u|,|v|,|z|≤1, show that every z with |z|≤1 satisfies |a z+b|≤2.
milestones.answer: For all |z|≤1, |a z+b|≤2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the bound is deduced directly by substituting u=a and v=b into the lemma.
hints: Apply the inequality with u=a and v=b.
Because |a|≤1, |b|≤1, and |z|≤1, the result is immediate.

milestones.description: Check whether the upper bound 2 can actually be attained. Test the specific polynomial f(z)=z^2+z-1/2 and the point z=1. Compute |f(z)| on |z|=1 and compute |a z+b| at z=1. Decide whether this example satisfies the hypothesis |f(z)|≤1 on |z|≤1 and whether it reaches the candidate bound 2.
milestones.answer: This test does not work: for f(z)=z^2+z-1/2, one gets |a·1+b|=|1+1|=2, but the polynomial does not satisfy |f(z)|≤1 on the unit disk, since f(1)=3/2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF they correctly reject this naive extremal attempt because the boundedness hypothesis fails.
hints: Evaluate f(1) first.
If |f(1)|>1, then the example cannot be used, even if |a z+b|=2 at some point.

milestones.description: Introduce the Möbius transform \phi_\alpha(w)=\dfrac{w-\alpha}{1-\overline{\alpha}w}, where \alpha=c=f(0). Since |f(z)|≤1 on |z|≤1, we have |c|≤1. Define F(z)=\phi_c(f(z))=\dfrac{f(z)-c}{1-\overline{c}f(z)}. Explain why F is analytic on |z|≤1, satisfies |F(z)|≤1 there, and has F(0)=0. Then state the Schwarz lemma conclusion for F.
milestones.answer: F is analytic on the unit disk, maps the unit disk to itself, and satisfies F(0)=0; hence by Schwarz lemma, |F(z)|≤|z| for |z|≤1 and |F'(0)|≤1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the response correctly sets up F and states the Schwarz lemma consequence |F'(0)|≤1. A full proof of Schwarz lemma is not needed.
decompose_advice: Differentiate F at 0 explicitly in terms of f'(0)=b and c.
Then use the same idea on a second transformed function to bring in a.

milestones.description: For F(z)=\dfrac{f(z)-c}{1-\overline{c}f(z)} with f(z)=a z^2+b z+c and |f(z)|≤1 on |z|≤1, compute F'(0) in terms of b and c. Using the Schwarz lemma conclusion |F'(0)|≤1, derive a sharper bound for b.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF they correctly differentiate the quotient at z=0 and conclude |b|≤1-|c|^2.
hints: Write F as \phi_c\circ f and use \phi_c'(c)=1/(1-|c|^2).
Since f'(0)=b, we get F'(0)=\phi_c'(c)f'(0).

milestones.description: Using the same transformed function F(z)=\dfrac{f(z)-c}{1-\overline{c}f(z)}, note that F(0)=0, so H(z)=F(z)/z is analytic on |z|<1 and satisfies |H(z)|≤1 there. Compute H(0) and H'(0) in terms of a,b,c by using the Taylor expansion of F at 0. Then apply the coefficient bound for bounded analytic functions on the unit disk to H to show |a+\overline{c}b^2/(1-|c|^2)|≤1-|c|^2, and combine this with |b|≤1-|c|^2 to deduce |a|+|b|≤1.
milestones.answer: From the expansion, H(0)=b/(1-|c|^2) and H'(0)=a/(1-|c|^2)+\overline{c}b^2/(1-|c|^2)^2. Since |H'(0)|≤1, we get |a+\overline{c}b^2/(1-|c|^2)|≤1-|c|^2. Using |b|≤1-|c|^2 gives |a|≤1-|c|^2 and hence |a|+|b|≤1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the response reaches the sharp inequality |a|+|b|≤1 by a valid expansion/bounded-coefficient argument. Minor algebraic differences are fine if equivalent.
decompose_advice: First expand F(z) up to the z^2 term explicitly.
Then define H(z)=F(z)/z and apply the coefficient bound separately to the constant and linear coefficients of H.

milestones.description: Assemble the established facts: for every polynomial f(z)=a z^2+b z+c with |f(z)|≤1 on |z|≤1, one has the sharp coefficient inequality |a|+|b|≤1. Therefore, for every z with |z|≤1, the triangle inequality gives |a z+b|≤|a||z|+|b|≤|a|+|b|≤1. Also, equality is attained by the admissible example f(z)=z, for which a=0, b=1, c=0, we have |f(z)|=|z|≤1 on |z|≤1, and |a z+b|=1 for all z. Conclude the range requested in the original problem.
milestones.answer: When |z|≤1, the range of |a z+b| is 0≤|a z+b|≤1; in particular, its maximum possible value is 1.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final conclusion states that |a z+b| cannot exceed 1 on the unit disk and that 1 is attainable. The original blank is typically filled by '≤1' or '[0,1]'.
hints: Use |a z+b|≤|a||z|+|b| and then |z|≤1.
Check the extremal example f(z)=z.

milestones.description:
Rewrite the quadratic form
Q(x,y,z)=x^{2}+2y^{2}+3z^{2}+2xy+2mzx+2nyz
as x^T A x for x=(x,y,z)^T, where A is a real symmetric 3×3 matrix. State the matrix A and restate the goal as a condition on A that guarantees Q(x,y,z)\ge 0 for all real x,y,z.
milestones.answer: A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&m\\1&2&n\\m&n&3\end{pmatrix}, and the problem is to find all real n such that A is positive semidefinite for every fixed m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3].
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the symmetric matrix is exactly identified and the equivalence with positive semidefiniteness of A is stated.
hints: In a symmetric quadratic form, the coefficient of 2xy is the (1,2) and (2,1) entry, similarly for 2mzx and 2nyz.

milestones.description:
Let A be a real symmetric 3×3 matrix. Use Sylvester's criterion for positive semidefiniteness in the following concrete form: A is positive semidefinite if and only if all principal minors of A are nonnegative. For the matrix
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&m\\1&2&n\\m&n&3\end{pmatrix}, list all principal minors that must be nonnegative.
milestones.answer: The required principal minors are: 1, 2, 3, \det\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}=1, \det\begin{pmatrix}1&m\\m&3\end{pmatrix}=3-m^2, \det\begin{pmatrix}2&n\\n&3\end{pmatrix}=6-n^2, and \det A.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF all 1×1, 2×2, and the full 3×3 principal minors are listed correctly.
hints: For a 3×3 symmetric matrix, the principal minors come from selecting the same set of row and column indices: {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {1,2,3}.

milestones.answer: Since 1,2,3, and 1 are positive, and 3-m^2\ge 0 because m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3], the remaining nontrivial conditions are 6-n^2\ge 0 and \det A\ge 0.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF it concludes exactly that only 6-n^2\ge0 and \det A\ge0 remain after using the given range of m.
hints: Use m^2\le 3 from m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3].

milestones.description:
For
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&m\\1&2&n\\m&n&3\end{pmatrix}, compute the determinant \det A explicitly as a polynomial in m and n.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF either expanded form 3-n^2-2m^2+2mn or completed-square form (3-m^2)-(n-m)^2 is obtained correctly; BEST if both are shown equivalent.
hints: Expand along the first row or use direct 3×3 determinant computation, then complete the square in n.

milestones.description:
Use the determinant identity
\det A=(3-m^2)-(n-m)^2
from the matrix
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&m\\1&2&n\\m&n&3\end{pmatrix}
to convert the condition \det A\ge 0 into an explicit interval condition on n in terms of m.
milestones.answer: \det A\ge 0 \iff (n-m)^2\le 3-m^2 \iff m-\sqrt{3-m^2}\le n\le m+\sqrt{3-m^2}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the inequality is solved correctly for n as a closed interval centered at m.
hints: Because m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3], the quantity 3-m^2 is nonnegative, so taking square roots is valid.

milestones.description:
Assume m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3] and n satisfies
m-\sqrt{3-m^2}\le n\le m+\sqrt{3-m^2}.
Prove directly that the 2×2 principal minor condition 6-n^2\ge 0 is then automatic, by finding the maximum possible value of |n| under that interval condition.
milestones.answer: From |n-m|\le\sqrt{3-m^2}, we get |n|\le |m|+\sqrt{3-m^2}. For |m|\le\sqrt3, the maximum of |m|+\sqrt{3-m^2} is \sqrt6 (attained when |m|=\sqrt{3/2}), so |n|\le\sqrt6 and hence n^2\le 6. Therefore 6-n^2\ge 0 is automatic.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF it validly derives n^2\le6 from the interval condition; equivalent optimization arguments are fine.
decompose_advice: First isolate the inequality |n-m|\le\sqrt{3-m^2} from the interval condition.
Then bound |n| by |m|+\sqrt{3-m^2}.
Finally maximize t+\sqrt{3-t^2} for t\in[0,\sqrt3] or square after substituting t=|m|.

milestones.description:
Show the converse implication needed for equivalence: if the inequality
x^{2}+2y^{2}+3z^{2}+2xy+2mzx+2nyz\ge 0
holds for all real x,y,z, then the interval condition
m-\sqrt{3-m^2}\le n\le m+\sqrt{3-m^2}
must hold. Use only the facts that this implies the symmetric matrix
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&m\\1&2&n\\m&n&3\end{pmatrix}
is positive semidefinite, hence all principal minors are nonnegative, especially \det A\ge 0, and that \det A=(3-m^2)-(n-m)^2.
milestones.answer: If the inequality holds for all x,y,z, then A is positive semidefinite, so \det A\ge 0. Since \det A=(3-m^2)-(n-m)^2, we get (n-m)^2\le 3-m^2, which is equivalent to m-\sqrt{3-m^2}\le n\le m+\sqrt{3-m^2}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF it proves necessity of the same interval condition from positive semidefiniteness and the determinant formula.
hints: This is just reversing the determinant argument: PSD implies nonnegative determinant.

milestones.answer: If m=0, then -\sqrt3\le n\le\sqrt3. If m=\pm\sqrt3, then 3-m^2=0 so n=m, giving the single values n=\sqrt3 or n=-\sqrt3 respectively.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF both endpoint checks are correct and consistent with the determinant formula.
hints: Substitute the given m-values directly into the interval.

milestones.description:
Assemble the previous facts for the matrix
A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1&m\\1&2&n\\m&n&3\end{pmatrix}:
- The inequality holds for all real x,y,z exactly when A is positive semidefinite.
- For this symmetric 3×3 matrix, positive semidefiniteness is equivalent to all principal minors being nonnegative.
- Because m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3], the principal minors 1,2,3,1,3-m^2 are already nonnegative.
- The determinant is \det A=(3-m^2)-(n-m)^2.
- The condition \det A\ge0 is equivalent to m-\sqrt{3-m^2}\le n\le m+\sqrt{3-m^2}.
- Under that interval condition, 6-n^2\ge0 is automatic.
Conclude the exact range of n requested in the original problem.
milestones.answer:
For each fixed m\in[-\sqrt3,\sqrt3], the inequality holds for all real x,y,z if and only if
m-\sqrt{3-m^2}\le n\le m+\sqrt{3-m^2}.
So the required range is
\boxed{n\in\left[m-\sqrt{3-m^2},\;m+\sqrt{3-m^2}\right]}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final answer is exactly the closed interval for n in terms of m, with iff/equivalence indicated.
hints: No new computation is needed: combine the PSD criterion, the determinant formula, and the automatic 6-n^2\ge0 check.

milestones.description: Let X be the number of heads obtained in 70 independent fair coin flips. Write the probability distribution of X, and express the quantities p and q from the problem in terms of X.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the binomial model with parameters 70 and 1/2 is stated and p,q are correctly rewritten as events on X.
hints: Each sequence of 70 flips has probability 2^-70.
The event 'more than 42 heads' means X>=43, and 'no more than 28 heads' means X<=28.

milestones.description: For X ~ Binomial(70, 1/2), prove the symmetry identity P(X=k)=P(X=70-k) for every integer k with 0<=k<=70.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer uses both the binomial formula and the identity C(70,k)=C(70,70-k).
hints: Use the explicit formula P(X=k)=C(70,k)(1/2)^k(1/2)^(70-k).
Then use the combinatorial identity C(70,k)=C(70,70-k).

milestones.description: Assume a random variable X satisfies P(X=k)=P(X=70-k) for all integers k from 0 to 70. Rewrite the event {X<=28} as an equivalent event for the variable 70-X, and then as an event involving X again.
milestones.answer: {X<=28} is equivalent to {70-X>=42}, so by symmetry q=P(X<=28)=P(X>=42).
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the event transformation X<=28 <=> 70-X>=42 is shown and then converted back to P(X>=42) using symmetry.
hints: If X<=28, then subtracting from 70 gives 70-X>=42.
Because X and 70-X have the same distribution under the given symmetry, probabilities of matching events are equal.

milestones.description: Using only the facts p=P(X>=43) and q=P(X>=42), compute p-q by comparing these two tail probabilities directly.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the nested-event subtraction is done correctly: P(X>=42)=P(X=42)+P(X>=43).
hints: Since {X>=43} is contained in {X>=42}, their difference is the single layer {X=42}.

milestones.description: For X ~ Binomial(70, 1/2), compute P(X=42) exactly using the binomial probability formula.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the exact binomial mass at k=42 is given; C(70,42)/2^70 and C(70,28)/2^70 are equivalent.
hints: Use P(X=k)=C(70,k)/2^70 with k=42.
No decimal approximation is needed.

milestones.description: Check the sign of p-q without doing any new computation: compare the events {X>42} and {X<=28} after using symmetry to rewrite q as a tail probability.
milestones.answer: Since q=P(X>=42) and p=P(X>=43), we have q>=p, so p-q<=0, consistent with p-q=-P(X=42).
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the response notes q=P(X>=42) includes the extra case X=42, so the difference must be nonpositive.
hints: The event {X>=42} contains {X>=43}.
Their probability difference should be exactly the missing probability at X=42, which is nonnegative.

milestones.description: Show that the two exact forms C(70,42)/2^70 and C(70,28)/2^70 are equal, so either may be used in the final answer.
milestones.answer: They are equal because C(70,42)=C(70,28).
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the symmetry of binomial coefficients C(n,r)=C(n,n-r) is invoked with n=70 and r=42.
hints: This is the same symmetry used in the distribution.

milestones.description: Use these already established facts: X ~ Binomial(70,1/2); p=P(X>=43); q=P(X<=28); symmetry gives q=P(X>=42); therefore p-q=-P(X=42); and P(X=42)=C(70,42)/2^70. Assemble them to give the final value of p-q.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final answer is exactly -C(70,42)/2^70, or equivalently -C(70,28)/2^70.
hints: Substitute q=P(X>=42) into p-q.
Then replace P(X=42) by its binomial formula.

milestones.description: Let the base triangle lie in the plane z=0 with coordinates K=(-5,0,0), L=(5,0,0), and M=(0,5\sqrt{3},0), so that triangle KLM is equilateral with side length 10. Let N=(x,y,h), where h>0 is the perpendicular distance from N to the base plane. Use the volume formula for pyramid KLMN, namely V=\frac13\cdot [KLM]\cdot h, and the fact that the area of an equilateral triangle of side 10 is 25\sqrt{3}. Determine h from the given volume 75.
milestones.answer: h=3\sqrt{3}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the height from N to plane KLM is found as 3√3 by 75=(1/3)(25√3)h.
hints: Compute the base area first: [KLM]=(\sqrt3/4)\cdot 10^2=25\sqrt3.
Then solve 75=\frac13\cdot 25\sqrt3\cdot h.

milestones.description: In the coordinate setup K=(-5,0,0), L=(5,0,0), M=(0,5\sqrt{3},0), N=(x,y,3\sqrt{3}), and T the midpoint of segment MN, write the coordinates of T explicitly in terms of x and y.
milestones.answer: T=\left(\frac{x}{2},\frac{y+5\sqrt3}{2},\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\right).
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF T is the average of M and N.
hints: Use the midpoint formula coordinatewise on M=(0,5√3,0) and N=(x,y,3√3).

milestones.description: For any tetrahedron with one face chosen as the base, if the apex has perpendicular height h above the base plane and a point T is the midpoint of the segment joining the apex to one vertex of the base, then the tetrahedron formed by replacing the apex with T has volume exactly half the original volume. Apply this fact to tetrahedra KLMN and KLNT, where T is the midpoint of MN, to determine the volumes of tetrahedra KLMT and KLNT.
milestones.answer: V(KLMT)=V(KLNT)=\frac{75}{2}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF both volumes are given as 75/2 with a correct midpoint/height-halving argument.
decompose_advice: First prove that the distance from T to plane KLM is half the distance from N to plane KLM.
Then for KLNT, use base KLN and note that T lies on segment MN with M in plane KLN, so T is at half the height from N to plane KLN.

milestones.description: For a tetrahedron, the inradius r satisfies r=\frac{3V}{S}, where V is the volume and S is the total surface area. Here V(KLMT)=V(KLNT)=75/2. If the inscribed sphere radii of tetrahedra KLMT and KLNT are equal, deduce that their total surface areas are equal. Then cancel the common face areas [KLT] and [KLM]=[KLN? no], being careful to compare the correct tetrahedra, to derive a relation among the remaining face areas. Write the final area identity only in terms of areas of triangles KMT, LMT, KLN, KNT, and LNT.
milestones.answer: [KMT]+[LMT]=[KLN]+[KNT]+[LNT].
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the equality of inradii is converted to equality of total surface areas, yielding [KLM]+[KMT]+[LMT]=[KLN]+[KNT]+[LNT], and then [KLM]=[KLT]+[?] is NOT required; the intended final relation is exactly [KMT]+[LMT]=[KLN]+[KNT]+[LNT] after canceling the common face [KLT] and using [KLM] on the left only as part of the total area expression for KLMT. Small algebraic slips should be rejected unless the final identity is correct.
decompose_advice: Write the four faces of tetrahedron KLMT explicitly: KLM, KLT, KMT, LMT.
Write the four faces of tetrahedron KLNT explicitly: KLN, KLT, KNT, LNT, then equate total areas because the volumes and inradii are equal.

milestones.description: Use vector cross products to express each area in the identity [KMT]+[LMT]=[KLN]+[KNT]+[LNT] in terms of x and y, under the coordinates K=(-5,0,0), L=(5,0,0), M=(0,5\sqrt3,0), N=(x,y,3\sqrt3), and T=(x/2,(y+5\sqrt3)/2,3\sqrt3/2). Show that these areas simplify to [KMT]=\frac14[KMN], [LMT]=\frac14[LMN], [KNT]=\frac12[KMN], and [LNT]=\frac12[LMN]. Also compute [KLN] explicitly from base KL and height from N to line KL.
milestones.answer: The area identity becomes [KLN]=\frac14([KMN]-[LMN]).
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF all four midpoint-based area reductions are obtained and substituted to reach [KLN]=([KMN]-[LMN])/4. Equivalent absolute-value formulations are acceptable if later specialized consistently.
decompose_advice: For triangles with vertex T on segment MN, compare their areas to the corresponding triangles with vertex N and the same base; midpoint implies a factor 1/2 in altitude.

Because [KMT] and [KNT] use the same line KM or KN? Compute directly or note that T divides MN in ratio 1:1, giving a factor 1/2 relative to triangles with vertex N or M; be explicit for each triangle.

milestones.description: Using K=(-5,0,0), L=(5,0,0), M=(0,5\sqrt3,0), N=(x,y,3\sqrt3), compute the areas [KMN], [LMN], and [KLN] as explicit square roots in x and y. Then use the relation [KLN]=\frac14([KMN]-[LMN]) to derive an equation involving only x and y. Simplify it to a circle or line condition as far as possible.
milestones.answer: [KMN]=\frac12\sqrt{(5\sqrt3-y)^2+3(x+5)^2+675}, [LMN]=\frac12\sqrt{(5\sqrt3-y)^2+3(x-5)^2+675}, [KLN]=5\sqrt{y^2+27}; and the area condition is 20\sqrt{y^2+27}=\sqrt{(5\sqrt3-y)^2+3(x+5)^2+675}-\sqrt{(5\sqrt3-y)^2+3(x-5)^2+675}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the three area formulas are correct and substituted into the previous identity correctly. Algebraic equivalents are fine.
decompose_advice: Use area of triangle ABC as \frac12\| (B-A)\times (C-A)\|.
For [KLN], since KL has length 10 and lies on the x-axis, the distance from N=(x,y,3√3) to line KL equals \sqrt{y^2+(3√3)^2}.

milestones.description: Let \theta be the dihedral angle between faces KLM and KLN along edge KL. In the chosen coordinates, the base face KLM is z=0 and line KL is the x-axis. The dihedral angle equals the angle between the lines in the two face planes perpendicular to KL; equivalently, in the yz-plane it is the angle between vectors (0,1) and (y,3\sqrt3). Show that \tan\theta=\frac{3\sqrt3}{|y|}. Then use the area equation from the previous milestone to solve for all possible y-values and hence all possible \theta.
milestones.answer: y=\pm \frac{9}{\sqrt{13}}, so \tan\theta=\sqrt{13}; hence \theta=\arctan(\sqrt{13}).
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the unique dihedral angle is found as arctan(√13). Equivalent forms such as cosθ=1/√14 are acceptable. The y-values should satisfy the area condition.
decompose_advice: Square the equation from the previous milestone carefully to eliminate radicals; symmetry suggests only y matters in the final dihedral angle.
After solving for y, use tanθ=(3√3)/|y|.

milestones.description: Assume additionally that faces KLM and LMN are perpendicular. Since plane KLM is z=0, a normal vector to plane KLM is (0,0,1). A normal vector to plane LMN can be obtained from vectors LM and LN. Impose perpendicularity of the planes by setting the dot product of these normals to 0, and derive a linear condition on x and y.
milestones.answer: y=\frac{5\sqrt3}{3}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the perpendicular-plane condition gives y=5√3/3.
hints: Compute a normal to plane LMN as LM×LN and require its z-component to be 0, since it must be perpendicular to (0,0,1).

milestones.description: Under the extra condition y=5\sqrt3/3 and the earlier equal-inradius condition, use the solved value |y|=9/\sqrt{13} from part (a) or re-solve consistently to determine x. Then compute the edge length MN from M=(0,5\sqrt3,0) and N=(x,5\sqrt3/3,3\sqrt3). Give all possible values.
milestones.answer: x=\pm \frac{20}{\sqrt{13}}, and MN=\sqrt{x^2+\left(\frac{10\sqrt3}{3}\right)^2+(3\sqrt3)^2}=\frac{5\sqrt{91}}{3\sqrt{13}}=\frac{5\sqrt{1183}}{39}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF x=±20/√13 and the corresponding single length MN is computed correctly. Equivalent simplified radical forms are acceptable.
decompose_advice: Check that y=5√3/3 is compatible with |y|=9/√13 by deriving x directly from the area equation if needed; do not assume incompatible values.
Then use the distance formula MN^2=x^2+(y-5√3)^2+(3√3)^2.

milestones.description: Assemble the established results: the equal-inradius condition together with volume 75 and the midpoint T leads to the unique dihedral angle \theta between faces KLM and KLN along KL satisfying \tan\theta=\sqrt{13}. Under the additional condition that faces KLM and LMN are perpendicular, the corresponding edge length MN is the value obtained from the coordinate computation. State the final answers to parts (a) and (b) exactly.
milestones.answer: a) The angle between the faces at edge KL is \arctan(\sqrt{13}) (equivalently, \cos\theta=1/\sqrt{14}). b) The possible value of MN is \frac{5\sqrt{1183}}{39}.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final response lists exactly the angle for part (a) and the length for part (b), with equivalent radical/trigonometric forms allowed.
hints: There is only one dihedral angle value because the sign of y does not change the angle.
In part (b), the two possible signs of x give the same edge length MN.

milestones.description: Restate the problem in formal terms. Let S={a,b,c,d} be four distinct positive integers. Condition (1) means there do not exist three distinct elements x<y<z of S with y-x=z-y. Let T={a+b,a+c,a+d,b+c,b+d,c+d}. A quadruplet is k-good if T contains k distinct numbers that themselves can be ordered as u,u+r,u+2r,...,u+(k-1)r for some positive integer r, and condition (1) also holds. State clearly what part (a) and part (b) ask for in this formal language.
milestones.answer: We need (a) one set of four distinct positive integers S with no 3-term arithmetic progression such that T contains 4 terms in arithmetic progression, and (b) the largest k for which some such S makes T contain k terms in arithmetic progression.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the two conditions are formalized correctly and the goals for parts (a) and (b) are correctly restated.
hints: A 3-term arithmetic progression in S means one element is the average of two others.
The six pairwise sums are exactly the elements of T.

milestones.description: Give an explicit example of four distinct positive integers with no three in arithmetic progression. Verify the claim directly from the four numbers. This is only a practice step for condition (1); the example does not yet need to satisfy anything about pairwise sums.
milestones.answer: For example, {1,2,4,8}. Its 3-element subsets are {1,2,4}, {1,2,8}, {1,4,8}, {2,4,8}; none is an arithmetic progression because the middle term is not the average of the other two in any subset.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF a valid 4-element set of distinct positive integers is given and all 3-element subsets are checked or an equivalent direct verification is provided.
hints: Powers of 2 are a safe source because gaps keep changing.
To check a 3-term progression, test whether twice one number equals the sum of the other two.

milestones.description: Order the quadruplet as a<b<c<d. Then the six pairwise sums satisfy a+b<a+c<a+d<b+c<b+d<c+d. Explain why any arithmetic progression contained in the six pairwise sums must therefore appear as a subsequence of this ordered list. Conclude that to search for long arithmetic progressions among the six sums, it is enough to study this ordered sequence of six numbers.
milestones.answer: Since adding larger numbers preserves order, the six pairwise sums are strictly ordered as a+b<a+c<a+d<b+c<b+d<c+d. Therefore any arithmetic progression contained in the set of pairwise sums is obtained by selecting some terms from this increasing list in increasing order, so long progressions can be studied within this ordered sequence.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the strict ordering is correct and the reduction to subsequences of the ordered sum list is stated.
hints: Use a<b<c<d and compare sums term-by-term.
A set of numbers in arithmetic progression becomes an increasing subsequence after sorting.

milestones.description: Construct a concrete 4-good quadruplet. Find distinct positive integers a<b<c<d such that no three of a,b,c,d form an arithmetic progression, and such that four of the six sums a+b,a+c,a+d,b+c,b+d,c+d form an arithmetic progression. Verify both properties explicitly.
milestones.answer: One example is (a,b,c,d)=(1,2,5,9). The set {1,2,5,9} has no 3-term arithmetic progression. The six sums are 3,6,10,7,11,14, so after sorting they are 3,6,7,10,11,14. The four sums 3,7,11,15 are not all present, so use instead (1,3,4,8): sums are 4,5,9,7,11,12; sorted 4,5,7,9,11,12, and 5,7,9,11 is a 4-term arithmetic progression. Also {1,3,4,8} has no 3-term arithmetic progression.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF a correct 4-good example is produced and both the no-3-AP condition and a 4-term AP among pairwise sums are explicitly checked. Reject the first trial if left uncorrected; accept the final valid example (1,3,4,8) or any other valid one.
hints: Try to force four sums to be equally spaced, for example by targeting a+c, b+c, a+d, b+d.
A valid example is (1,3,4,8): check the sums 5,7,9,11.

milestones.description: For the candidate quadruplet (1,3,4,8), verify condition (1) completely by checking each 3-element subset of {1,3,4,8}. State for each subset why it is not an arithmetic progression.
milestones.answer: The 3-element subsets are {1,3,4}, {1,3,8}, {1,4,8}, {3,4,8}. They are not arithmetic progressions because 3 is not the average of 1 and 4, 3 is not the average of 1 and 8, 4 is not the average of 1 and 8, and 4 is not the average of 3 and 8.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF all four 3-subsets are checked correctly, or an equivalent exhaustive verification is given.
hints: In a 3-term arithmetic progression x<y<z, the condition is 2y=x+z.
There are exactly four 3-element subsets of a 4-element set.

milestones.description: Assume a<b<c<d and write the ordered pairwise sums as s1=a+b, s2=a+c, s3=a+d, s4=b+c, s5=b+d, s6=c+d. Prove the identity s1+s6=s2+s5=s3+s4=a+b+c+d. Deduce that if all six sums s1,s2,s3,s4,s5,s6 formed a 6-term arithmetic progression, then the common difference would force s1,s2,s3,s4,s5,s6 to be symmetric about their common average (a+b+c+d)/2.
milestones.answer: The equalities are immediate: (a+b)+(c+d)=(a+c)+(b+d)=(a+d)+(b+c)=a+b+c+d. Hence opposite terms in the ordered list of six sums have the same total, so if all six formed a 6-term arithmetic progression, they would be symmetric about average (a+b+c+d)/2.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the three equal-sum identities are proved and the symmetry consequence for a hypothetical 6-term arithmetic progression is correctly stated.
hints: Pair the smallest and largest sums, then the next smallest and next largest, and so on.
Any finite arithmetic progression is symmetric about its average.

milestones.description: Show that k=6 is impossible. Assume for contradiction that for some distinct positive integers a<b<c<d with no three in arithmetic progression, all six pairwise sums s1=a+b, s2=a+c, s3=a+d, s4=b+c, s5=b+d, s6=c+d form a 6-term arithmetic progression in increasing order. Let the common difference be r. Then s2-s1=c-b, s3-s2=d-c, s4-s3=(b+c)-(a+d), s5-s4=d-c, s6-s5=c-b. Use equality of consecutive differences in an arithmetic progression to derive c-b=d-c, and then show this implies b,c,d form an arithmetic progression, contradicting condition (1).
milestones.answer: If s1,...,s6 is a 6-term arithmetic progression, then s2-s1=s3-s2, so c-b=d-c. Hence b,c,d are in arithmetic progression, contradicting condition (1). Therefore k≠6.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the contradiction c-b=d-c is obtained from equal consecutive differences and identified as making b,c,d a 3-term AP. Extra details about all differences are fine.
hints: Compute s2-s1 and s3-s2 explicitly.
Equality of these two consecutive gaps already gives the contradiction.

milestones.description: Show that k=5 is impossible. Assume a<b<c<d and that five of the six ordered sums s1=a+b<s2=a+c<s3=a+d<s4=b+c<s5=b+d<s6=c+d form a 5-term arithmetic progression. Since any 5-element subset of {s1,s2,s3,s4,s5,s6} omits exactly one term, handle the six possible omissions separately. In each case, use the requirement that the chosen five numbers have equal consecutive differences to derive that one of a,b,c,d is the average of two others, contradicting condition (1).
milestones.answer:
In every case, a contradiction arises:
- Omit s1: then s3-s2=s4-s3 gives d-c=(b+c)-(a+d), and s4-s3=s5-s4 gives (b+c)-(a+d)=d-c, which implies a+d=2c, so a,c,d are in AP.
- Omit s2: among s1,s3,s4,s5,s6, equal spacing gives s4-s3=s5-s4, so (b+c)-(a+d)=d-c, hence a+d=2c, contradiction.
- Omit s3: equal spacing in s1,s2,s4,s5,s6 gives s2-s1=s4-s2, so c-b=(b+c)-(a+c)=b-a, hence a,b,c are in AP.
- Omit s4: equal spacing in s1,s2,s3,s5,s6 gives s3-s2=s5-s3, so d-c=(b+d)-(a+d)=b-a, and also s6-s5=c-b=d-c, giving b,c,d in AP or a,b,d aligned to force a contradiction.
- Omit s5: equal spacing in s1,s2,s3,s4,s6 gives s2-s1=s3-s2, so c-b=d-c, hence b,c,d are in AP.
- Omit s6: equal spacing in s1,s2,s3,s4,s5 gives s2-s1=s3-s2, so c-b=d-c, hence b,c,d are in AP.
Therefore k≠5.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF all omission cases are addressed and each yields a contradiction with condition (1). Minor variation in which equal gaps are compared is fine, as long as every case is covered rigorously.
decompose_advice: Split into six separate atomic milestones, one for each omitted sum case.
For each case, explicitly write the five selected sums in increasing order and equate the relevant consecutive differences.

milestones.description: Use the following established facts: (i) the quadruplet (1,3,4,8) has no three elements in arithmetic progression, and its pairwise sums 4,5,7,9,11,12 contain the 4-term arithmetic progression 5,7,9,11, so a 4-good quadruplet exists; (ii) k=6 is impossible because if all six pairwise sums formed an arithmetic progression, then c-b=d-c, making b,c,d an arithmetic progression; (iii) k=5 is impossible because any choice of five of the six ordered pairwise sums leads, by equal-gap conditions, to some three of a,b,c,d being in arithmetic progression. Combine these to answer parts (a) and (b) exactly.
milestones.answer: a) A 4-good quadruplet is (1,3,4,8). b) The maximal k is 4.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final answer gives a valid 4-good quadruplet for part (a) and states that the maximum possible k is 4 for part (b).
hints: Existence of k=4 comes from the explicit example.
Impossibility of k=5 and k=6 shows no larger k can occur, since there are only six pairwise sums.

milestones.description: Let A_n be a convex polygon with n vertices, where n is an integer at least 3. A diagonal is a segment joining two nonadjacent vertices. The polygon sides together with all diagonals are drawn, and no three diagonals meet at one interior point. Restate the two targets in counting language: first count all diagonals of A_n, and then count all triangles whose three sides lie entirely on drawn segments (polygon sides or diagonals) and whose interiors are regions determined by this drawing.
milestones.answer: Count (1) all segments joining nonadjacent vertex pairs; count (2) all triangular regions in the full drawing of sides and diagonals.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer correctly formalizes both counting goals and mentions the no-three-diagonals-concurrent condition for the full drawing.
hints: A side joins adjacent vertices; a diagonal joins nonadjacent vertices.
The second target is about triangles created by the arrangement of all drawn segments, not just triangles with vertices among the polygon vertices.

milestones.description: In a convex n-gon, every pair of distinct vertices determines exactly one segment. There are C(n,2) total segments joining vertex pairs. Exactly n of these are polygon sides, because the polygon has n edges. Use this to find the number of diagonals.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the number of diagonals is given as C(n,2)-n or n(n-3)/2.
hints: Count all vertex pairs, then remove adjacent pairs.

milestones.description: Consider a fixed side AB of a convex n-gon. A triangle in the full drawing can use AB as one of its sides only if its third vertex is one of the other polygon vertices, because every drawn segment has endpoints at polygon vertices. How many distinct triangles have AB as one side and have their other two sides drawn among the polygon sides and diagonals?
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer is n-2 with the explanation that the third vertex can be any of the other n-2 vertices.
hints: Choose any vertex other than A and B as the third vertex.
Convexity guarantees the triangle lies inside the polygon.

milestones.description: To count all triangles formed by the sides and diagonals of a convex n-gon with no three diagonals concurrent, classify each such triangle by the number k of its sides that lie on polygon sides, where k can be 0, 1, 2, or 3. Explain why every triangle formed in the drawing belongs to exactly one of these four classes, and why counting each class separately will count every triangle exactly once.
milestones.answer: Partition the triangles into four disjoint classes according to k = 0,1,2,3 sides lying on polygon sides; summing the four class counts gives the total number of triangles.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer gives the disjoint classification by k and states that the total is the sum over the four classes.
hints: Each triangle has exactly three sides, and each side is either part of a polygon side or part of a diagonal.
The value of k is uniquely determined for each triangle.

milestones.description: Count triangles in the full drawing of a convex n-gon that have exactly 2 polygon sides as sides of the triangle. Any such triangle must use two adjacent polygon sides meeting at one polygon vertex, together with the diagonal joining their other endpoints. Conversely, every choice of three consecutive vertices gives exactly one such triangle. Find the number of these triangles.
milestones.answer: n.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer is n, with equivalent reasoning that each vertex determines one triangle formed by its two incident sides and the diagonal between neighboring vertices.
hints: Pick the middle vertex of three consecutive vertices on the polygon.
There is one such triangle at each polygon vertex.

milestones.description: Count triangles in the full drawing of a convex n-gon that have exactly 1 polygon side as a side of the triangle. Fix a polygon side AB. Any triangle having AB as its only polygon side is determined by choosing a third polygon vertex C that is not adjacent to A or B; then AC and BC are diagonals, not polygon sides. For a fixed side AB, count such choices of C, and then sum over all n polygon sides.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer is n(n-4), or equivalent reasoning: for each side there are n-4 valid third vertices.
hints: For side AB, exclude A and B themselves and also the two vertices adjacent to A and B on the outside of side AB.
That leaves n-4 choices for the third vertex.

milestones.description: A triangle in the full drawing of all sides and diagonals of a convex n-gon can have exactly 3 polygon sides as its sides if and only if the polygon is a triangle itself. For n>3, prove that no triangle in the drawing can have all 3 sides equal to polygon sides. State the resulting count of such triangles for general n.
milestones.answer: The count is 1 when n=3, and 0 when n>3.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the milestone states and justifies that only the whole polygon in the case n=3 has three polygon sides; otherwise impossible.
hints: Three polygon sides form a closed 3-cycle only when the polygon has exactly 3 vertices.
In an n-gon with n>3, polygon sides follow the boundary and do not close up after only three edges.

milestones.description: Count triangles in the full drawing of a convex n-gon that have exactly 0 polygon sides as sides of the triangle. Such a triangle must be bounded entirely by three diagonals. Show that choosing any 6 distinct polygon vertices in cyclic order determines exactly one such triangle: the triangle formed by the three pairwise intersections of the diagonals joining opposite vertices of the 6 chosen points. Conversely, every triangle bounded by 3 diagonals arises from exactly one 6-tuple of vertices in this way. Use this bijection to count these triangles.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the answer is C(n,6) with a correct bijection between 0-side triangles and 6 chosen vertices in cyclic order.
decompose_advice: First prove existence: from 6 chosen vertices v1,v2,v3,v4,v5,v6 in cyclic order, the diagonals v1v4, v2v5, v3v6 intersect pairwise and form one central triangle.
Then prove uniqueness: any triangle bounded by 3 diagonals uses 6 distinct diagonal endpoints, and these 6 vertices reconstruct the triangle uniquely.

milestones.description: Check the class counts for small n. Use the formulas: diagonals = n(n-3)/2; triangles with 2 polygon sides = n; triangles with 1 polygon side = n(n-4); triangles with 3 polygon sides = 1 if n=3 and 0 if n>3; triangles with 0 polygon sides = C(n,6). Verify the total triangle count for n=3, n=4, and n=5.
milestones.answer: n=3: 1 triangle; n=4: 4 triangles; n=5: 10 triangles.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF these three checkpoint totals are correct and consistent with the class formulas.
hints: For n=3, only the polygon itself appears.
For n=4, the total is 4+0+0=4.
For n=5, the total is 5+5+0=10 because C(5,6)=0.

milestones.description: Assemble the final answers using the established class counts. The number of diagonals in a convex n-gon is C(n,2)-n = n(n-3)/2. The triangles formed by the full drawing split into four disjoint classes: exactly 2 polygon sides contributes n triangles, exactly 1 polygon side contributes n(n-4) triangles, exactly 0 polygon sides contributes C(n,6) triangles, and exactly 3 polygon sides contributes 1 when n=3 and 0 when n>3. Combine these to give the final count of triangles of A_n.
milestones.answer: (1) The number of diagonals is n(n-3)/2. (2) The number of triangles formed by the sides and diagonals is C(n,6)+n(n-3), with the n=3 case giving 1 as well.
milestones.note: ACCEPT IF the final answers are exactly these: diagonals n(n-3)/2 and triangles C(n,6)+n(n-3) (equivalently n+n(n-4)+C(n,6), with the n=3 edge case consistent).
hints: For n>3, add n + n(n-4) + C(n,6).
This simplifies to n(n-3)+C(n,6).
